items.followUp: State four differences between plant and animal cells.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the nuclear organisation of the two cell types.
rubric.description: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus and have a nucleoid; eukaryotes have a true nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for stating the contrasting nuclear organisation of both cell types.

rubric.why: Identifies whether membrane-bound organelles are present.
rubric.description: Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have them.
rubric.how: Award for stating the correct contrast.

rubric.why: States a key difference in the form or association of their DNA.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic DNA is usually circular and naked; eukaryotic nuclear DNA is linear and associated with proteins.
rubric.how: Award for giving either the contrasting DNA forms or the contrasting DNA associations.

rubric.why: Distinguishes their relative size and complexity.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller and simpler; eukaryotic cells are generally larger and more complex.
rubric.how: Award for stating either the size contrast or the complexity contrast.

modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus and have a nucleoid; eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles.
Prokaryotic DNA is usually circular and naked; eukaryotic nuclear DNA is linear and associated with proteins.
Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller and simpler; eukaryotic cells are generally larger and more complex.

rubric.why: Identifies enzymes as biological catalysts.
rubric.description: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly made of proteins.
rubric.how: Award for identifying enzymes as biological catalysts.

rubric.why: Explains how enzymes affect reactions.
rubric.description: They lower activation energy and increase the rate of biochemical reactions.
rubric.how: Award for stating that enzymes lower activation energy and speed reactions.

rubric.why: Recognises the specificity of enzyme action.
rubric.description: Each enzyme is specific for a particular substrate or reaction.
rubric.how: Award for stating that an enzyme acts specifically on a substrate or reaction.

rubric.why: States that enzymes remain available after catalysis.
rubric.description: Enzymes are not used up during reactions and can be reused.
rubric.how: Award for stating that enzymes are not consumed and can be reused.

rubric.why: Recognises that enzyme activity depends on conditions.
rubric.description: Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; unsuitable conditions may denature it.
rubric.how: Award for stating the optimum conditions or that unsuitable conditions can denature enzymes.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly made of proteins.
They lower activation energy and increase the rate of biochemical reactions.
Each enzyme is specific for a particular substrate or reaction.
Enzymes are not used up during reactions and can be reused.
Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; unsuitable conditions may denature it.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and functions of the small intestine.

rubric.why: Describes the stomach's general form and position.
rubric.description: The stomach is a J-shaped muscular sac situated in the upper abdomen, mainly on the left side.
rubric.how: Award for stating its shape or muscular-sac structure together with its position.

rubric.why: Identifies the stomach's connections.
rubric.description: It receives food from the oesophagus and opens into the duodenum; sphincters regulate passage.
rubric.how: Award for naming both the oesophagus and duodenum as the stomach's connections.

rubric.why: Names important gastric secretions.
rubric.description: Gastric glands produce gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid, pepsin and protective mucus.
rubric.how: Award for naming the gastric glands and acid and pepsin, or for naming acid, pepsin and mucus.

rubric.why: Explains the stomach's mechanical role in digestion.
rubric.description: The muscular walls churn and mix food with gastric juice, forming semi-liquid chyme.
rubric.how: Award for describing the churning or mixing of food and the formation of chyme.

rubric.why: States an important function of the stomach.
rubric.description: The stomach begins protein digestion, helps kill bacteria and temporarily stores food.
rubric.how: Award for any one stated stomach function with its associated secretion where applicable.

modelAnswer: The stomach is a J-shaped muscular sac situated in the upper abdomen, mainly on the left side.
It receives food from the oesophagus and opens into the duodenum; sphincters regulate the passage of food.
Gastric glands in its wall secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid, pepsin and protective mucus.
The muscular walls churn and mix food with gastric juice, forming semi-liquid chyme.
Pepsin begins protein digestion, hydrochloric acid provides an acidic medium and helps kill bacteria, and the stomach temporarily stores food.

items.followUp: Describe the composition and functions of blood cells.

rubric.why: Describes the appearance and nature of plasma.
rubric.description: Plasma is the straw-coloured liquid part of blood.
rubric.how: Award for identifying plasma as the straw-coloured liquid part of blood.

rubric.why: Gives the major component of plasma.
rubric.description: Plasma consists mainly of water, about 90–92%.
rubric.how: Award for stating that water is the main component and giving an approximate proportion.

rubric.why: Names important plasma proteins.
rubric.description: Plasma proteins include albumin, globulins and fibrinogen.
rubric.how: Award for naming at least two of the plasma proteins.

rubric.why: States a transport or clotting role of plasma.
rubric.description: Plasma transports dissolved substances around the body, and fibrinogen helps in blood clotting.
rubric.how: Award for a correct transport role or for linking fibrinogen with blood clotting.

modelAnswer: Blood plasma is the straw-coloured liquid part of blood.
It consists mainly of water, about 90–92%, with dissolved substances.
Its proteins include albumin, globulins and fibrinogen; it also contains salts, nutrients, hormones, gases and waste products.
Plasma transports nutrients, hormones and waste products around the body, and fibrinogen helps in blood clotting.

items.followUp: In an investigation, what is the difference between an independent variable and a dependent variable?

rubric.why: Describes the control group as the baseline without the tested treatment.
rubric.description: The control group does not receive the experimental treatment and provides a basis for comparison.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the control group lacks the treatment or serves as the comparison.

rubric.why: Describes the experimental group as receiving the tested treatment or factor.
rubric.description: The experimental group receives the treatment or is exposed to the factor being tested.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the experimental group receives the treatment or is exposed to the tested factor.

modelAnswer: The control group does not receive the experimental treatment and provides a basis for comparison.
The experimental group receives the treatment or is exposed to the factor being tested.
